title: A Spring as Expectation Under Tension
text: A spring is like expectation under tension: the farther reality is displaced from what is expected, the stronger the psychological pressure to restore consistency. Likewise, stretching or compressing a spring creates a restoring force that increases with displacement.

title: A Mechanical Ratchet as Commitment
text: A mechanical ratchet is like commitment: each completed step becomes psychologically difficult to reverse, so progress accumulates in one direction. Likewise, a ratchet permits motion tooth by tooth while mechanically preventing backward motion.

title: Mechanical Resonance as Emotional Triggering
text: Mechanical resonance is like emotional triggering: a small recurring stimulus can produce an unexpectedly large response when it matches an already sensitive psychological pattern. Likewise, repeated forces applied at a system’s natural frequency can build increasingly large mechanical oscillations.

title: A Mechanical Governor as Self-Control
text: A mechanical governor is like self-control: when behavior begins exceeding a desired level, an internal corrective process pushes it back toward a target. Likewise, a centrifugal governor automatically reduces a machine’s input when its rotational speed rises too far.

title: A Flywheel as Psychological Momentum
text: A flywheel is like psychological momentum: once a belief or intention is strongly established, it tends to keep thought moving in the same direction despite small disturbances. Likewise, a spinning flywheel stores rotational energy and resists sudden changes in speed.

title: A Gear Train as a Chain of Reasoning
text: A gear train is like a chain of reasoning: one thought constrains the next, transmitting an initial premise through a sequence of dependent transformations. Likewise, each gear transfers motion to the next, converting the original rotation into a predictable final motion.

title: Attention as a Movable Spotlight
text: Attention is like a movable spotlight: it illuminates a narrow region of a larger field, making whatever falls inside it easier to inspect. Moving the beam toward one target necessarily leaves other targets in relative darkness.

title: Cognitive Dissonance as a Misaligned Gear Train
text: Cognitive dissonance is like tension in a misaligned gear train: incompatible beliefs pull the system in directions that cannot smoothly coexist. The mind reduces the strain by adjusting, reinterpreting, or discarding one of the conflicting elements until the mechanism runs more smoothly.

title: Emotion Regulation as a Pressure-Control Valve
text: Emotion regulation is like a pressure-control valve: emotional pressure can build inside the system, while regulatory processes determine how quickly and through which channels it is released. A valve that is too open produces uncontrolled discharge, while one that is too tightly shut allows pressure to accumulate.

title: Habit as a Well-Worn Mechanical Track
text: Habit is like a well-worn mechanical track: repeated movement deepens the channel until the system naturally follows the same path with little guidance. Changing the behavior requires either blocking the old track or repeatedly forcing motion along a new one.

title: Working Memory as a Workbench
text: Working memory is like a workbench: only a few objects can be kept on its surface at once, while everything else must be stored elsewhere. Adding too many items causes interference, just as an overcrowded bench makes each task harder to perform.

title: Self-Control as a Mechanical Governor
text: Self-control is like a mechanical governor: it continuously detects when behavior is drifting away from a chosen target and applies corrective force. Strong self-control is therefore less like constant braking than like a well-tuned mechanism making small adjustments before large deviations occur.

title: Cellular Metabolism as a Production Economy
text: Cellular metabolism is like a production economy: cells allocate scarce inputs such as glucose, oxygen, and amino acids across competing biochemical pathways to produce energy, structures, and waste. Bottlenecks in one input can constrain total output even when other resources are abundant.

title: Immune System as an Insurance Market
text: The immune system is like an insurance market: it pays continuous costs to maintain defenses against uncertain future biological losses. Greater investment in surveillance and preparedness can reduce the expected damage from rare but costly infections.

title: Sexual Selection as an Auction Market
text: Sexual selection is like an auction market: individuals compete for reproductive opportunities using costly signals, displays, or resources, while potential mates discriminate among the available bids. Traits can become increasingly elaborate when success depends on relative attractiveness rather than sheer survival value.

title: Food Web as a Supply Chain
text: A food web is like a supply chain: energy and matter move through interconnected producers, consumers, and decomposers much as goods move through linked stages of production and exchange. Disruption at one node can propagate through the network and alter the viability of distant participants.

title: Gene Regulation as Taxes and Subsidies
text: Gene regulation is like a system of taxes and subsidies: regulatory molecules raise or lower the biochemical “cost” of expressing particular genes, shifting cellular resources toward some activities and away from others. Changing these incentives can reorganize cell behavior without changing the underlying genetic inventory.

title: Natural Selection as Market Competition
text: Natural selection is like market competition: organisms with traits better suited to local conditions leave more descendants, just as firms with better-fitting strategies tend to capture more demand. Over time, unsuccessful variants disappear while successful ones become more common.

title: Creative Destruction as Ecological Succession
text: Creative destruction is like ecological succession: New technologies and business models can displace established industries much as new species and ecological communities replace earlier ones after environmental change. The destruction of one economic structure simultaneously opens resources and niches for another.

title: Economic Specialization as Cell Differentiation
text: Economic specialization is like cell differentiation: Just as cells in a multicellular organism become specialized for tasks such as contraction, signaling, or digestion, workers and firms can specialize in particular productive functions. Specialization increases efficiency but also creates mutual dependence, because no single specialized unit can perform every function the larger system requires.

title: Market Competition as Natural Selection
text: Market competition is like natural selection: Firms with traits that fit consumer demand tend to survive and expand, while poorly adapted firms shrink or disappear. Profits and losses act like selective pressures, continually reshaping the population of businesses.

title: Inflation as a Rising Metabolic Rate
text: Inflation is like a rising metabolic rate: When money circulates faster than an economy’s capacity to produce goods and services, prices can rise just as a body generates more heat when its metabolism accelerates beyond its ability to dissipate energy. The faster circulation changes the system’s operating conditions even when its underlying physical resources have not increased proportionally.

title: Supply-and-Demand Adjustment as Biological Homeostasis
text: Supply-and-demand adjustment is like biological homeostasis: When a shortage pushes prices upward, producers are encouraged to supply more while consumers tend to demand less, much as biological feedback mechanisms counter deviations from an equilibrium. When a surplus appears, the feedback runs in the opposite direction.

title: Compound Interest as Exponential Population Growth
text: Compound interest is like exponential population growth: Just as organisms reproduce and their offspring later reproduce in turn, invested returns can generate additional returns of their own. Given enough time, repeated multiplication can make small initial quantities become very large.
